content.intro: Legacy maintenance preserves real behavior while removing risky assumptions. Use tests to make changes incremental, check the supported PHP/dependency matrix, and migrate deprecated patterns with a documented plan. In this lesson, focus on readme files; then compare it with installation instructions. Use the example to predict a result before checking it, and record one case where the behavior may differ.
content.why_it_matters: You will use documentation for php projects when building readable, testable PHP programs. Its practical value is knowing which rule applies, what result to expect, and how to handle failure or unexpected input.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Legacy maintenance preserves real behavior while removing risky assumptions. Use tests to make changes incremental, check the supported PHP/dependency matrix, and migrate deprecated patterns with a documented plan. For documentation for php projects, begin with readme files. Also distinguish installation instructions; configuration documentation; api documentation. Identify the input, the rule applied, and the observable output or side effect; then check the relevant official reference when a version or edge-case detail matters.

items.title: README files
items.text: Check the operation result, use a known storage boundary, and consider empty files, permissions, invalid paths, and cleanup.

items.title: Installation instructions
items.text: Know when to use installation instructions, what input or program state it changes, and which boundary case is worth testing.

items.title: API documentation
items.text: Expect network failures and malformed responses; validate the response, set bounded timeouts, and make repeat delivery safe where needed.

content_blocks.title: A small PHP example for Documentation for PHP Projects
content_blocks.code:
<?php
$file = tempnam(sys_get_temp_dir(), "php-course-");
if ($file === false) { throw new RuntimeException("Cannot create temp file"); }
file_put_contents($file, "ready\n");
echo trim((string) file_get_contents($file)) . PHP_EOL;
unlink($file);

content_blocks.title: Professional habit
content_blocks.text: Change legacy code incrementally, use tests to preserve behavior, and verify the target PHP/dependency compatibility matrix.

content_blocks.title: Walk through one example
content_blocks.text: Read the example for documentation for php projects from top to bottom. Start by identifying readme files, write down the relevant variable values or control-flow choice, and predict the expected output before running it. Then change one input or condition, check a boundary case, and explain why the result changed.

The learner can explain its input, rule, and observable output.

hints: Start with the most direct listed subtopic and a single input.
Keep the example small enough that you can predict the output manually.
Test one normal case and one empty, invalid, or boundary case.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a pattern without understanding its inputs and output.
common_mistakes.why: Small environment or type differences can change behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Trace one example by hand, name expected outputs, and consult version-matched official docs.

common_mistakes.problem: Ignoring empty, invalid, or boundary input.
common_mistakes.why: Real data rarely matches only the simplest example.
common_mistakes.fix: Add a deliberate edge-case check before relying on the result.

common_mistakes.problem: Making several changes at once while debugging.
common_mistakes.why: It becomes difficult to identify which change caused the behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Reduce the issue to one small reproducible case, change one cause, and retest.

summary: Documentation for PHP Projects is one part of the PHP implementation workflow.
Prefer explicit behavior and testable examples over implicit assumptions.
Change legacy code incrementally, use tests to preserve behavior, and verify the target PHP/dependency compatibility matrix.
